title: Can Your Neighbor Point a Camera at Your House? The Law Explained
excerpt: Neighbors can usually film what is plainly visible from their property, but not what you reasonably keep private. Where the line falls and what to do.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
In most states, yes — your neighbor can point a camera at your house, provided it stays aimed at what is plainly visible from their property. The law protects what anyone can see from a public spot, and it also protects what you reasonably expect to keep private. Nearly every neighbor-camera dispute is really an argument about which side of that line the lens sits on.

The rest of this guide explains where the line usually falls, what crosses it, and the exact steps to take if your neighbor's camera is aimed at your windows, your yard, or your family.

The rule that decides most disputes

The deciding concept is the reasonable expectation of privacy, and the mechanism is simple: if a person standing on the public sidewalk could see the same thing with their own eyes, recording it is usually allowed. If the camera does something your eyes cannot — tilt over a fence, zoom into a shaded window, amplify sound — it usually is not. There is no single federal law for neighbor cameras; a patchwork of state statutes, local ordinances, and privacy claims applies instead, which is why the same camera can be fine in one town and problematic in the next.

A camera that sees what a person on the sidewalk could see is usually legal. A camera that sees what a person could not see is where trouble starts.

What is usually allowed

  • Cameras on the neighbor's own property aimed at the street, sidewalk, or a shared driveway
  • Incidental capture of your front yard, walkway, or mailbox from a normal angle
  • Doorbell cameras facing the entrance and the path to it
  • Video — without audio — of outdoor areas visible from a public vantage point

What usually crosses the line

The window test

If the lens can see into a window you would reasonably expect to be private — especially bedrooms and bathrooms — the camera is aimed wrong. A camera that captures the inside of your home, even from a neighbor's porch, is the classic invasion-of-privacy setup. Angle matters more than distance: a camera across the street pointed straight at your living-room window is far more exposed than one pointed at the sky.

The audio problem

Modern camera microphones pick up conversation from surprising distances, and audio is where neighbor cameras most often cross into wiretapping territory. In all-party consent states, recording conversations without everyone's agreement can be illegal even outdoors. If your neighbor's camera can hear your backyard conversations, that is a separate issue from the video — and a serious one. See our hidden camera laws guide for how consent rules work.

What to do about it, step by step

  1. Document the camera: photograph it from several angles, note its direction, and log dates and times of anything it captures of your property.
  2. Talk to your neighbor first. Most disputes are about placement, not malice, and a calm request to adjust the angle resolves most cases.
  3. Check local ordinances and any HOA rules — many cities regulate camera placement, and HOAs often go further.
  4. Call the non-emergency police line if the camera captures genuinely private areas; officers can advise whether this is a privacy complaint or harassment.
  5. Consult a lawyer if the lens is aimed into your home, follows family members, or comes with other concerning behavior — invasion-of-privacy and harassment claims exist for exactly this.
  6. Fix your side regardless of the law: fencing, shrubs, window film, and curtains reduce what any camera can see.

When it stops being a neighbor problem

Escalate quickly if the camera is repositioned after you asked for it to be moved, if it follows a specific person, if it points at a child's window, or if footage is shared online. That pattern can turn a privacy dispute into harassment or stalking. Keep your documentation, file a police report, and ask a lawyer about protective orders or a civil invasion-of-privacy claim.

Everything above is general information. Privacy and surveillance laws vary by state and by municipality, including what counts as a private area, so check your own jurisdiction's rules before acting.
